summary: Agent C, revision 1.201: part 3 of the Indigenous histories split. New field community_engaged_indigenous (period_4 with roots from 1974; reviewed through 2022): description and scope from practitioners' own statements of method; five new strands (Cree oral history as source and method; relational methodologies; kinship, community and the archive; research ethics and governance; Indigenous historians' own institutions); nine new roster rows; a chronology of 34 events from the 1974 Yukon family request to Fraser and Stevenson (2022); and, by guarded moves, seven strands and seventeen roster rows from `indigenous` with their ids, sources and links. New packaged entry life_lived_like_a_story crediting Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith, Annie Ned and Julie Cruikshank (three edges, six dated events; method and authorship only). Four person entries: Winona Wheeler (five edges, twelve events), Brenda Macdougall (two edges, nine events), Robert Alexander Innes (three edges, eight events; his 2018 critique of historians of the starvation policy and of Daschuk) and Mary Jane Logan McCallum (three edges, one held for stage 2; eight events). Six field edges; four existing edges rerouted to the new field (edge_696, edge_697, edge_698 by source; edge_776 by target and target strand, with a revised note). Thirty-five new ihc_ sources, three source addenda, four new people records, and people updates for nine records (node links and minimal identity notes). Drafted under the OCAP limits and with the OCAP review's cuts applied (items 1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 12).

edge_776.relationship: Stó:lō community–university practice that its teachers call a 'new ethnohistory': collaborative, reflexive, with community-set questions and results returned to the Stó:lō archives
edge_776.map_label: A new ethnohistory with the Stó:lō
edge_776.evidence_note: Stó:lō community and university participants combine different research resources in this particular field-school programme. This comparison records overlapping practice; it does not make either field the origin of the other. Revision 1.201 (rerouted from `indigenous` to community_engaged_indigenous): read in full in a Wayback capture of the authors' posting, Carlson, Lutz and Schaepe (2009) write that 'A new type of ethnohistory was called for' (p. 1), that 'The new ethnohistory is collaborative with the people we are trying to understand, and brings mutual benefits' (p. 3), and that field-school papers and interviews go to the Stó:lō archives (p. 5).

text_revisions.old: Three elders and an anthropologist collaborate; life interviewing and transmitted traditions remain distinct practices.
text_revisions.new: Three elders and an anthropologist collaborate; life interviewing and transmitted traditions remain distinct practices. The families asked for the recording in 1974; the narrators chose to tell their lives through stories, songs and oratory, and Cruikshank selected and ordered the texts (McClellan 1992). See the packaged entry Life Lived Like a Story.

text_revisions.old: Community priorities, cultural teaching, archives and university instruction contribute different resources. Planning in 1997 preceded the first class in 1998; elders, hosts and students also participated.
text_revisions.new: Community priorities, cultural teaching, archives and university instruction contribute different resources. Planning in 1997 preceded the first class in 1998; elders, hosts and students also participated. The teachers call it a 'new ethnohistory': 'collaborative with the people we are trying to understand', with community staff and members setting topics 'beneficial to the community', and papers and interviews going to the Stó:lō archives to 'help build capacity' (Carlson, Lutz and Schaepe 2009, pp. 3–5). The 2018 volume describes community-engaged scholarship that 'invites members of the Indigenous community themselves to identify the research questions' (publisher).
later accounts (2009, 2011, 2016); Historical Atlas (2001); Towards a New Ethnohistory (2018)

text_revisions.old: Family knowledge, scholarly dialogue and mentorship shape historical practice; the roles remain distinct.
text_revisions.new: Family knowledge, scholarly dialogue and mentorship shape historical practice; the roles remain distinct. Leddy, a member of the Serpent River First Nation, found the university ethics process 'culturally inappropriate': it defines Aboriginal participants as a 'vulnerable group', distancing an Aboriginal researcher from her own community. 'We have our own methodologies and ethical practices' (2010, pp. 3, 13–15).

text_revisions.old: Leddy cites Wheeler (2005), Smith (1999), Wilson (1998) and Cruikshank with the three Yukon elders (1991 edition), among others.
text_revisions.new: Leddy cites Wheeler (2005), Smith (1999, quoted at pp. 140 and 191), Wilson (1996 and 1998), Innes (2009) and Cruikshank with the three Yukon elders (1991 printing), among others.

text_revisions.old: Leddy cites her relational account of oral history; the cited chapter itself remains unread.
text_revisions.new: Cree historian who treats Indigenous oral history 'as source and method' and asks historians to build 'reciprocal relationships' with elders and 'apply the teachings' (2010); Leddy takes her words as the epigraph for community-based history (2010). Her 2005 chapter remains unread.

text_revisions.old: Reflections on the Social Relations of Indigenous Oral Histories (2005), as cited by Leddy (2010)
text_revisions.new: Cree Intellectual Traditions in History (2010); Reflections on the Social Relations of Indigenous Oral History (2005, unread; cited by Leddy 2010)

text_revisions.old: Historical research within her own Serpent River community joins scholarly and family relationships.
text_revisions.new: Anishinabe kwe historian of her own Serpent River First Nation; historical research joins scholarly and family relationships, and she argues that university ethics review, which treats Aboriginal participants as a 'vulnerable group', distances Indigenous researchers from their communities (2010).

text_revisions.old: Anthropologist and collaborator in a southern Yukon life-history project; the elders are knowledge producers, not anonymous source material.
text_revisions.new: Anthropologist and collaborator in a southern Yukon life-history project, begun at the families' request in 1974; the elders are knowledge producers, not anonymous source material (see the packaged entry).
